tools.title: What Did the Interview Actually Tell You?
tools.summary: An interview observes behavior. Hiring predicts future work. What connects the two?

examples.name: ML evaluation
examples.title: They spotted a problem. Did it change their recommendation?
examples.scenario: You’re hiring an ML engineer who will help decide whether models are ready to ship. In the interview, you show a classifier with 92% accuracy and ask whether the team should deploy it. The candidate says there could be data leakage: information available during testing might not be available when the model is used.
examples.impression: “They spotted leakage. They have good evaluation judgment.”
examples.tension: That could be true. But naming a familiar problem and knowing what to do about it are different pieces of evidence.
examples.comparisonTitle: What happens after they name the problem?

comparison.label: What you observe
values: They mention possible leakage, then recommend deploying because 92% sounds high.
They ask how the test data was separated, propose checking performance on later data, and hold off on recommending deployment until that check is done.

comparison.label: What this supports
values: They recognize the term. This answer gives little evidence that they would use it to challenge a release decision.
They connect a concern to a test and a release condition. That supports a more specific expectation: they may question an unreliable evaluation before recommending release.

examples.takeawayTitle: Look for what the concern changes
examples.takeaway: A concern becomes more useful evidence when it changes the proposed test, the recommendation, or the next action. Saying “there may be leakage” tells you less than showing how that possibility changes the decision.
examples.boundedConclusion: “In this case, they turned an evaluation risk into a concrete check before release. I’d expect them to contribute to model reviews, with help on our domain’s metrics. I haven’t yet seen whether they do the same with an unfamiliar problem.”
examples.followup: Give them a different evaluation scenario and ask what would make them change their recommendation. Look for whether they adapt the reasoning rather than repeat the same test.

examples.name: System design
examples.title: They don’t know our queue. What does that tell us?
examples.scenario: You’re hiring a backend engineer to work on a service that uses a message queue. The candidate hasn’t used your queue product. You still need to understand whether they can reason about failures, repeated messages, and recovery.
examples.impression: “They don’t know our stack. They’ll struggle with reliability.”
examples.tension: Unfamiliarity with a product is visible. Their ability to reason about reliability needs its own evidence.
examples.comparisonTitle: Two different reasons you might lack confidence
columns: You observed a problem in the reasoning

comparison.label: What happened in the interview
values: You asked which queue products they had used, but never discussed delivery failures or repeated messages.

You explained that the queue can deliver a message more than once. Even after discussing the consequences, they kept a design that could charge the customer twice and offered no way to prevent or detect it.

comparison.label: What you can conclude
values: You know they lack experience with this product. You don’t yet know how they reason about these failures.
You have evidence of difficulty handling this failure mode in this discussion. The concern is more specific than unfamiliarity with the product.

examples.takeawayTitle: “We didn’t see it” and “they struggled with it” are different
examples.takeaway: An interview that never tested failure handling leaves a question open. An answer that overlooks a failure after it has been explained gives you something concrete to examine. Neither warrants a broad claim about every aspect of the candidate’s ability.
examples.boundedConclusion: “They’ll need to learn our queue. Before judging their reliability skills, I’d discuss a duplicate-message scenario and ask how they would prevent repeated side effects. Product experience and failure reasoning are separate questions.”
examples.followup: Explain the delivery behavior without requiring product-specific vocabulary. Ask them to trace one message through a failure and recovery. Then assess the reasoning against the role’s expectations.

discussion.label: Evidence
discussion.question: What did we observe?
discussion.explanation: Describe the action or answer before giving it a meaning.
discussion.example: They questioned the test split and proposed evaluating on later data before recommending release.

discussion.label: Expectation
discussion.question: What work might they handle, with what support?
discussion.explanation: Translate the observation into a specific work expectation. Name the help it assumes.
discussion.example: I’d expect them to contribute to model reviews, with guidance on our domain’s metrics.

discussion.label: Uncertainty
discussion.question: What remains untested, and how would we check it?
discussion.explanation: Name the limit of the prediction and a next step that could change your confidence.
discussion.example: We haven’t seen this reasoning on an unfamiliar problem. Use a different evaluation scenario in a follow-up discussion.

related.title: Decision-Complete
related.reason: Inspect the path from evidence to judgment.

related.title: From Intuition to Argument
related.reason: Turn a broad impression into a claim others can examine.

tools.discussionTemplate: We observed [specific behavior]. That gives us reason to expect [work contribution], with [support]. We’re still unsure about [gap], which we could check by [next step].
introduction: A technical interview shows how someone responds to a particular problem. Hiring asks us to predict their contribution on real work, with our team’s support and constraints.
The jump from an encouraging answer to a broad expectation can hide assumptions. Separate what you saw, what it suggests, and what remains untested.

lessons.title: Look for consequences.
lessons.text: The ML example asks whether recognizing a risk changes the candidate’s test or recommendation—not just whether they can name the problem.

lessons.title: Identify the actual gap.
lessons.text: The queue example separates product knowledge from failure reasoning. An untested capability and an observed difficulty need different follow-ups.

lessons.title: Keep predictions conditional.
lessons.text: Neither example establishes performance across unfamiliar problems. Name the support and conditions your expectation assumes so it can be questioned and revisited.

tools.title: What Does This Result Let Us Decide?
tools.summary: Fewer overnight pages. A successful migration rehearsal. Both sound promising. What would you recommend next?
tools.cardSummary: An on-call engineer wants fewer overnight pages. A team wants to move its database. Explore what the results let them do next.
tools.problemTitle: The numbers look good. The next step is less clear.
introduction: A promising result arrives with a caveat. Is it a reason to stop, a reason to narrow the plan, or something to check before going further?
Follow two engineering decisions. In each one, change what the team knows or needs—and see why the recommendation changes.
tools.frameworkBoundary: The reader needs to see how the observation supports the action—and where that support ends.
tools.examplesDisclaimer: Two fictional situations. Explore the detail that changes each decision.
tools.discussionSummary: How this could sound in the report
tools.templateGap: If a part is missing, decide whether you need analysis, an explanation, evidence, or agreement on a trade-off.
tools.caution: A recommendation can be to continue, narrow the scope, retain the current approach, or collect specific evidence. State what the uncertainty permits or prevents.
tools.discussionTemplate: We found [result] on [cases]. That supports [interpretation], but leaves [gap]. Given [what the next step requires], I recommend [action and scope].

discussion.label: Observation
discussion.question: What changed, compared with what, and on which cases?
discussion.example: Raising the timeout threshold would reduce last week’s pages from 18 to 4.

discussion.label: Interpretation
discussion.question: What does that establish, and what remains uncertain?
discussion.example: That establishes fewer interruptions. Replaying a real checkout outage shows the proposed rule would also miss a problem customers experienced.

discussion.label: Decision
discussion.question: Given our requirements, what should we do next?
discussion.example: Keep the current threshold while revising the rule. Check the revision against known outages before using it to page the on-call engineer.

lessons.title: Name the decision criterion.
lessons.text: The on-call team wants fewer unnecessary interruptions while still detecting customer problems. Counting pages answers only part of that question.

lessons.title: Make the caveat change something.
lessons.text: The migration rehearsal does not cover the archive. Whether that stops the next move depends on whether the archive has to move with it.

lessons.title: Identify the work that remains.
lessons.text: An unclear result needs analysis. An unclear connection needs explanation. An untested assumption needs evidence. A disputed trade-off needs a decision from the responsible person.

related.title: Decision-Complete
related.reason: Inspect the path from evidence to a defensible action.

related.title: What Did the Metric Throw Away?
related.reason: Ask whether an omitted distinction could change the choice.

examples.name: Overnight pages
examples.title: Eighteen pages. Four worth waking up for?
scenario: It is 2 a.m. The on-call engineer gets another page from the checkout service. More than 1% of requests have timed out for five minutes. By the time they open the dashboard, the spike has passed.
The team has received 18 timeout pages in a week. Someone proposes raising the timeout threshold to 5%. Applied to last week’s traffic, that rule would have sent just four pages.
examples.impression: “Four pages instead of eighteen. Let’s raise the threshold.”
examples.tension: That would mean fewer interrupted nights. But would the new rule still wake someone when customers cannot complete a purchase?
examples.comparisonTitle: What did counting pages leave open?

comparison.label: Question
values: How many pages would the new rule send?
Would it still detect outages that need a response?

comparison.label: Finding
values: Four pages instead of eighteen on last week’s traffic.
During Thursday’s checkout outage, 3% of requests timed out. The proposed 5% rule would never have paged.

options.label: Only the number of pages
options.title: A quieter night is promising. Detection is still an open question.
options.evidence: The new rule would have sent four pages last week. Nobody has checked whether the pages it removes include incidents that needed a response.
options.recommendation: Keep the current rule for now. Replay known outages against the proposed threshold and check whether it would alert soon enough for the team to respond.
options.reason: The useful next check is about what the rule would miss. Another count of pages cannot answer that.

options.label: They also replayed Thursday’s checkout outage
options.title: The quieter rule would have missed a real outage.
options.evidence: On Thursday, 3% of checkout requests timed out long enough for customers to lose purchases. The current rule paged the engineer. A 5% threshold would not have paged at all.
options.recommendation: Do not adopt this threshold. Keep the current rule while looking for a way to filter brief spikes without hiding sustained checkout failures, then replay known incidents again.
options.reason: Fewer pages was a real improvement in one measure. The replay shows why that improvement does not justify this change.

examples.takeaway: Fewer pages tells us about interruptions. To recommend this rule, we also need to know what happens to incident detection. Writing the recommendation exposes the part the first measurement did not answer.
examples.boundedConclusion: “The proposed threshold would reduce last week’s pages from 18 to 4, but it would also miss Thursday’s checkout outage. I recommend keeping the current rule while we revise how it filters brief spikes. The quieter rule does not meet our need to detect sustained customer failures.”
examples.followup: Find a revised rule that distinguishes brief spikes from sustained failures. Replay known incidents and inspect detection time before changing the production alert.

examples.name: Migration scope
examples.title: The rehearsal passed. Why is the migration still on hold?
scenario: The team has spent weeks preparing to move its order database. In the rehearsal, recent orders arrive intact: totals match, relationships hold, and the application reads them correctly. The team wants to schedule the move.

Then someone asks about the archive. Older orders use a different schema, and none were included in the rehearsal. A colleague says the migration should stop until every historical format has been tested.
examples.impression: “We haven’t tested the archive. We can’t move anything yet.”
examples.tension: The gap is real. But does the archive have to move this weekend, or can it stay where it is while recent orders move first?
examples.comparisonTitle: The same rehearsal can support different migration plans

comparison.label: Requirement
values: The application can safely route recent and historical queries to the correct database. The archive stays available in the old system.
The application requires recent and historical records in the new database at the same time.

comparison.label: What the evidence supports
values: A staged migration of the tested record types, provided routing, consistency checks, and rollback are verified.
The recent-record rehearsal does not establish that older schemas will migrate correctly. Test representative historical records before the full move.

interaction.question: What does the next move actually require?

options.label: The archive can stay; split access and rollback are verified
options.title: The archive can wait. A limited move has support.
options.evidence: The recent-order rehearsal passed. The team has also verified that the application can access orders across both databases consistently and that it can roll back. Historical formats remain untested.
options.recommendation: Move the tested recent orders in stages and monitor the agreed checks. Keep the archive in the old database until its formats have been rehearsed.
options.reason: The gap limits which records can move. It does not, by itself, rule out the smaller move the team can safely support.

options.label: The application needs all orders in the new database
options.title: This move needs evidence the rehearsal did not provide.
options.evidence: The recent-order rehearsal still passes. But the application cannot operate with the archive left behind, and historical formats remain untested.
options.recommendation: Hold the full migration. Rehearse representative historical formats, resolve failures, and verify the checks and rollback plan before scheduling the move.
options.reason: The same caveat now concerns records required for the next step. It blocks this plan, even though the recent-order result remains valid.

examples.takeaway: “The archive is untested” describes a limit of the rehearsal. Its consequence depends on the plan: it may restrict the move to recent orders, or prevent the full move from going ahead.
examples.boundedConclusion: “The rehearsal supports moving the tested recent orders. Because split access and rollback are verified, I recommend a staged move while the archive stays in the old database. This is not evidence that historical formats are ready to migrate.”
examples.followup: Confirm which records the next step actually requires. For a staged move, verify split access and consistency; for a full move, rehearse representative older schemas as well.

items.rule: The first page makes clear what question the document answers.
items.why: The reader should know what problem the document is solving before seeing details.

items.rule: The document is written for a specific reader or decision.
items.why: A report for a technical reviewer, manager, or business stakeholder should not emphasize the same details.

items.rule: Each section has one clear job.
items.why: Problem Summary sets up the question. Method explains how it was measured. Results show what was found. Analysis explains what it means. Conclusion states what should happen next.

items.rule: The method, sample, and scope are stated before the results.
items.why: The reader needs to know what was evaluated before interpreting the numbers.

items.rule: The document states what was not evaluated or what the results do not prove.
items.why: This prevents the reader from overclaiming the findings.

items.rule: Each section opens with 1–2 sentences before the first table, figure, or list.
items.why: Readers need context before they encounter evidence.

items.rule: Every table or figure is introduced in the prose with the finding it supports.
items.why: “Figure 2 shows…” is not enough. The sentence should say what the figure shows.

items.rule: Every caption states the takeaway or purpose of the table/figure.
items.why: A good caption helps the reader understand why the evidence is included.

items.rule: Every percentage has a visible denominator.
items.why: “8%” is unclear unless the reader knows 8% of what.

items.rule: Percentages in the same table use the same denominator, or the table explains when they do not.
items.why: Mixed denominators make numbers look comparable when they may not be.

items.rule: If categories can overlap, the table says so.
items.why: Otherwise, readers may assume the rows add up to 100%.

items.rule: Each analytical paragraph follows: claim → evidence → consequence.
items.why: The consequence sentence is what turns a result into analysis.

items.rule: Each paragraph makes one main claim.
items.why: Multiple claims in one paragraph make the logic hard to follow.

items.rule: Prose explains what the numbers mean; it does not simply repeat the table.
items.why: Repeating the table adds length without adding insight.

items.rule: Comparisons name both sides explicitly.
items.why: “Better,” “higher,” or “longer” is unclear without a baseline.

items.rule: Qualitative words are replaced with specific claims when possible.
items.why: Words like “important,” “significant,” and “helpful” are weak unless tied to evidence or action.

items.rule: For each claim about why a change was necessary, name the most obvious counterargument and address it.
items.why: If the report doesn't preempt that question, it looks like the author didn't think of it.

items.rule: The executive summary can be understood without reading the full body.
items.why: A busy reader should still understand the main finding, implication, and next step.

items.rule: The conclusion answers: what was found, why it matters, and what should happen next.
items.why: A conclusion should not only summarize; it should guide action.

items.rule: Every recommendation is supported by evidence from the document.
items.why: Recommendations that do not follow from the results feel unsupported.

items.rule: Read the document once for flow, not grammar. Each section should naturally lead to the next.
items.why: A technically correct document can still feel confusing if the logic does not progress clearly.

items.rule: The executive summary gives the answer, not an introduction to the document. A reader who stops here should understand the main finding.
It states why the finding matters to this reader or decision. Importance should not be left for the reader to infer.
It states the recommended action or decision, when one is required. The reader should know what should happen next.
It includes only the evidence needed to support those points. Methodological and supporting detail belongs in the body unless it changes the decision.
